new_statements.quote: In Mazateco the stress falls mechanically on the final syllable of a word (this applies, also, to the nouns already listed) and need not be indicated by any orthographic device. The stressed syllable of a dissyllabic word is noticeably longer in duration than the unstressed one that precedes it. The glides of unstressed syllables may be pronounced with extreme rapidity, so rapidly that it is very hard to hear them.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress = fixed final; Pike states exactly that ('falls mechanically on the final syllable of a word') and adds the length correlate and that stress is predictable/unmarked. The lect is the Huautla de Jiménez dialect ('the dialect represented here being that of Huautla de Jimenez, Oaxaca. The data concerning it were gathered by me in collaboration with Miss Eunice Victoria Pike and Mrs. George Cowan, from 1936-45', file), which is the variety huau1238 denotes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is automatic (non-contrastive) and falls on the last syllable of every word, including nouns; the stressed final syllable is longer than the preceding unstressed one, and unstressed syllables can be very reduced. Pike therefore leaves stress unmarked in his orthography; tone (four levels) is the contrastive prosodic feature.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the passage read.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; 'mechanically' and 'this applies, also, to the nouns already listed' assert full regularity. (The scope of 'word' with respect to enclitics is not addressed in this passage; Pike & Pike 1947 IJAL, already held by the project, treat enclitics as stressless and grouped with the preceding word.)
new_statements.identity_note: Pike 1948 explicitly describes the Mazateco of Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca (Highland Mazatec), data gathered 1936-45 with Eunice V. Pike and Florence Cowan; this is the variety Glottolog huau1238 (Huautla Mazatec) covers, so the statement is about the catalog language, not a sister Mazatec variety.

tone_statements.quote: Mazatec has both level and contour tones. Some dialects have three level tones (Jalapa de Díaz) while others have up to four (Huautla, San Miguel Soyaltepec). The ALFALEIM convention for writing tones is the following: High (/H/) represented with an acute accent (í) Mid-high (/h/) represented with a grave accent (ì) Mid (/M/) which is not represented (i) Low (/L/) represented with an underlining (i)

sources.note: Per Vielma Hernández 2017: in Huautla Mazatec there are about a dozen morphemes whose only residue of a syllable is a tone (floating tone), realised only when preceded by a morpheme ending in high tone, e.g. 'niños' ʂti 3-4 in isolation vs thĩ 1 'hay' + ʂti 3-4 -> thĩ 1-4 ʂti 3-4.

sources.note: Per the SIL record: 'Survey of then investigated tonal contrasts in Mexican languages'. Per Vielma Hernández 2017: describes eighteen Mexican tone languages including Huautla de Jiménez Mazatec, for which she counts thirteen tone groups ('trece grupos tonales'), and notes that change of aspect and person is frequently signalled by tone change.

sources.note: Per Vielma Hernández 2017: states that tone is a fundamental element of Mazatec and recognises four tone registers: high, mid-high, mid-low and low ('cuatro registros tonales: alto, medio alto, medio bajo y bajo'); also describes tense-aspect prefixes and the two-stem verb pattern.

tone.says: Title and secondary citations only: a diasystemic (cross-dialect) study of Mazatec verbal tonal inflection; Klint 2025 (UNAM diss., pp. 383-384 and ch. on verb tone) cites it for the view that 'no existe un tono asociado al núcleo mismo, sino que cada celda en el paradigma de un verbo sigue patrones melódicos específicos (Léonard y Fulcrand 2016)' and groups it with L&F 2018/2019 as inflection-class analyses across the Mazatec 'diasistema'; Chávez Peón & Filio 2021 cite it for *w > /β, b/ betac…
